lessons.title: Scaffolding Fundamentals for African Construction Sites
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 2 of the Scaffolding training programme. This lesson introduces the core principles that every scaffolder, site supervisor, and construction manager in Africa must understand before erecting any scaffold. Scaffolding is a temporary structure that supports workers, materials, and equipment at height. In Africa, where rapid urbanisation is driving high-rise construction in cities like Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg, and Cairo, scaffolding competence is not optional. It is a legal, safety, and commercial necessity. A poorly built scaffold can collapse, injure workers, delay projects, and expose your company to lawsuits and regulatory shutdowns. A well-built scaffold keeps productivity high and workers safe. The first fundamental is understanding load capacity. Every scaffold has a designed load limit. There are three main categories: light-duty scaffolds for painting and electrical work, medium-duty scaffolds for general construction, and heavy-duty scaffolds for masonry and concrete work. In many African markets, materials are often moved manually, which means scaffolds may be subjected to uneven and dynamic loads. You must calculate the total load including workers, tools, materials, and the weight of the scaffold itself. Never exceed the safe working load. The second fundamental is stability. Scaffolds must be braced in both longitudinal and transverse directions. Base plates and sole boards distribute weight and prevent sinking into soft ground, which is common during rainy seasons in West and Central Africa. On sloped ground, you must use adjustable base jacks and never rely on loose bricks or stones for levelling. The third fundamental is the foundation. Before erecting any scaffold, inspect the ground. Remove debris, compact loose soil, and use timber sole boards at least 50mm thick and 200mm wide. In sandy or waterlogged areas, you may need concrete pads or steel base plates with larger surface area. The fourth fundamental is access and egress. Workers must be able to get on and off the scaffold safely. Use internal ladders or dedicated access towers. Never allow workers to climb the outside of the scaffold frame. In Africa, where many sites lack proper stair towers, this is a common cause of falls. The fifth fundamental is edge protection. Guardrails, mid-rails, and toe boards must be installed on all open sides and ends. The top guardrail should be between 950mm and 1100mm above the platform. Mid-rails should be about halfway. Toe boards prevent tools and materials from falling onto workers below, which is critical in congested urban sites. The sixth fundamental is inspection and tagging. Every scaffold must be inspected before first use, after any alteration, after bad weather, and at regular intervals. Use a colour-coded tag system: green for safe, yellow for caution, red for do not use. This simple system saves lives and is easy to implement even on remote sites. The seventh fundamental is training and supervision. Scaffolding is not a job for untrained labourers. In many African countries, enforcement of training standards varies, but responsible contractors must ensure that scaffolders are trained and competent. Supervisors must understand scaffold design, load limits, and inspection requirements. The eighth fundamental is personal protective equipment. Hard hats, safety harnesses, non-slip boots, and gloves are essential. Harnesses must be anchored to a reliable point, not to the scaffold itself unless it is designed for that purpose. The ninth fundamental is housekeeping. Keep platforms clear of unnecessary materials, tools, and debris. A cluttered scaffold is a dangerous scaffold. The tenth fundamental is planning. Before erecting, plan the scaffold layout, the sequence of erection, the materials needed, and the dismantling procedure. A written scaffold plan should be available on site. In Africa, where supply chains can be unpredictable, planning also means ensuring you have enough couplers, boards, and tubes before starting. This lesson has covered the ten fundamentals: load capacity, stability, foundation, access, edge protection, inspection, training, PPE, housekeeping, and planning. In the next lesson, we will look at the different types of scaffolding systems and how to choose the right one for your project. Remember, scaffolding is a life-safety structure. Treat it with the respect it deserves.

lessons.title: Types of Scaffolding Systems and Selection Criteria
lessons.body: In this lesson, we examine the main types of scaffolding systems used across Africa and the factors that determine which system is best for a given project. Choosing the right system affects safety, speed, cost, and labour requirements. The first type is tube and coupler scaffolding. This system uses steel tubes and separate couplers to connect them. It is flexible and can be adapted to complex shapes, which makes it popular in Africa for renovation work, curved buildings, and sites with irregular access. However, it requires skilled labour and takes longer to erect. Couplers must be tightened to the correct torque, usually around 40 to 65 Newton metres, and checked regularly. The second type is modular or system scaffolding. This includes cuplock, kwikstage, ringlock, and similar systems. These use prefabricated frames and locking mechanisms. They are faster to erect, require less skilled labour, and have built-in safety features like guardrail posts. In African cities with tight project schedules, modular scaffolding is increasingly preferred. It is also easier to inspect because connections are standardized. The third type is frame scaffolding. This uses prefabricated frames with cross-bracing. It is simple and quick to assemble, often used for low-rise buildings, painting, and light construction. Frame scaffolding is common in smaller African towns where access to advanced systems is limited. However, it is less adaptable to complex shapes and may not be suitable for heavy-duty work. The fourth type is mobile scaffolding. These are towers on castors or wheels. They are ideal for indoor work, maintenance, and short-duration tasks. In Africa, mobile scaffolds are used in warehouses, shopping malls, and factories. The key safety rule is to lock the castors before climbing and never move the scaffold while workers are on it. The fifth type is suspended scaffolding. This includes swing stages and rope access platforms. They are used for high-rise facade work, window cleaning, and external painting. Suspended scaffolds require rigorous inspection of ropes, anchors, and hoists. In Africa, where high-rise construction is booming, suspended scaffolds are common but must be operated by trained personnel only. The sixth type is cantilever scaffolding. This is used where the ground cannot support a standard scaffold, such as over water, roads, or deep excavations. Cantilever scaffolds rely on strong anchor points and counterweights. They require engineering design and must never be improvised. The seventh type is birdcage scaffolding. This is a dense grid of tubes and boards used for large ceiling areas, such as auditoriums, churches, and industrial halls. It is common in African religious and community buildings. Birdcage scaffolds must be designed to carry the weight of workers and materials and must have proper access and egress. Now let us look at selection criteria. The first criterion is the nature of the work. Light work like painting needs light-duty scaffolding. Heavy work like block laying needs heavy-duty scaffolding. The second criterion is the height and shape of the building. Tall buildings need modular or suspended systems. Complex shapes need tube and coupler. The third criterion is the duration of the project. Short projects may use mobile or frame scaffolding. Long projects justify investment in modular systems. The fourth criterion is ground conditions. Soft or sloped ground requires base plates, sole boards, or cantilever systems. The fifth criterion is access to materials and skills. In remote African sites, tube and coupler may be the only option because modular systems are not available. The sixth criterion is cost. Tube and coupler has lower initial cost but higher labour cost. Modular systems have higher initial cost but lower labour cost and faster erection. The seventh criterion is regulatory requirements. Some African countries have specific standards for scaffolding, often based on British, European, or South African standards. You must comply with local regulations. The eighth criterion is wind loading. In coastal areas like Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, and Lagos, wind can be strong. Scaffolds must be designed to resist wind, and ties to the building must be adequate. The ninth criterion is seismic activity. In North Africa and parts of East Africa, seismic design may be required. The tenth criterion is availability of trained personnel. The best system is useless if no one knows how to erect it safely. In summary, there is no single best scaffolding system. The right choice depends on the work, the site, the skills, and the budget. Always consult a competent person or engineer for complex projects. In the next lesson, we will cover erection and dismantling procedures.

lessons.title: Safe Erection and Dismantling Procedures
lessons.body: This lesson focuses on the practical steps for erecting and dismantling scaffolding safely on African construction sites. Erection and dismantling are the most dangerous phases because the structure is incomplete and workers are exposed. A systematic approach reduces risk and improves efficiency. Before erection begins, conduct a site survey. Identify ground conditions, overhead power lines, underground services, and access routes. Overhead power lines are a major hazard in African cities where informal wiring is common. Maintain a safe distance, usually at least 3 metres for low voltage and more for high voltage. If you cannot maintain distance, isolate the power or use insulated barriers. Next, prepare the foundation. Clear the area, level the ground, and place sole boards. Sole boards should be at least 50mm thick and 200mm wide. Use base plates on top of sole boards. For soft ground, use larger pads or concrete blocks. For sloped ground, use adjustable base jacks. Never use bricks or stones for levelling. Then, plan the sequence. Start from the lowest point and work upwards. Erect the first bay, then the second, and so on. Install ledgers, transoms, and braces as you go. Do not leave the scaffold partially braced overnight. If you must stop work, secure the structure and tag it as incomplete. During erection, workers must wear harnesses and attach to a safe anchor point. On many African sites, harnesses are available but not used correctly. Supervisors must enforce harness use. Use a tool belt or rope to hoist tools and materials. Never throw tools or materials. Install guardrails and toe boards as soon as the platform is in place. Do not wait until the end. Ties to the building are critical. Use tie tubes and anchors at regular intervals, both horizontally and vertically. The general rule is one tie for every two bays horizontally and every two lifts vertically. Ties prevent the scaffold from collapsing in wind or due to impact. For modular scaffolds, follow the manufacturer instructions. Do not mix components from different systems unless approved by an engineer. Mixing systems is a common cause of failure in Africa where materials are scarce. For tube and coupler scaffolds, tighten couplers to the correct torque. Use a torque wrench and check a sample of couplers daily. Loose couplers can slip and cause collapse. Access ladders must be secured and extend at least 1 metre above the platform. Use internal ladders where possible. Do not use the scaffold bracing as a ladder. During dismantling, reverse the erection sequence. Remove ties last, not first. Remove guardrails and toe boards only when the platform below is ready to receive the workers. Lower materials using ropes or mechanical hoists. Never throw materials from height. Dismantling must be supervised by a competent person. The area below must be cordoned off. Use warning signs and barriers. In congested African markets, pedestrians may ignore barriers, so use additional flag persons if necessary. Weather is a major factor. Do not erect or dismantle scaffolds in strong winds, heavy rain, or thunderstorms. In West Africa, the rainy season can bring sudden storms. Monitor weather forecasts and secure the scaffold before storms. After erection, inspect the scaffold before use. Check base plates, couplers, ties, guardrails, toe boards, and access. Use a checklist. Tag the scaffold green if safe. If any defect is found, tag it red and do not use until repaired. During use, inspect daily and after any event that may affect stability. Keep a record of inspections. In many African countries, regulators may ask for inspection records after an incident. Good records protect your company. Training is essential. Scaffolders must be trained in the specific system they are using. A tube and coupler scaffolder may not be competent with ringlock. Provide refresher training regularly. Supervisors must also be trained. They must know how to check couplers, ties, and foundations. They must have the authority to stop work if conditions are unsafe. Emergency procedures must be in place. If a scaffold collapses or a worker falls, there must be a rescue plan. Do not rely on calling emergency services in remote areas. Have a stretcher, first aid kit, and trained first aiders on site. In summary, safe erection and dismantling require planning, competent workers, correct materials, and strict supervision. Follow the sequence, install ties and guardrails early, and never take shortcuts. In the next lesson, we will cover inspection, maintenance, and tagging systems.

lessons.title: Inspection, Maintenance, and Tagging Systems
lessons.body: This lesson covers the inspection, maintenance, and tagging of scaffolding. These are ongoing activities that ensure the scaffold remains safe throughout its service life. In Africa, where many sites operate with tight budgets and limited regulatory oversight, a robust inspection and tagging system is one of the most cost-effective safety measures you can implement. The first concept is the pre-use inspection. Before any worker steps onto a scaffold, a competent person must inspect it. The inspection should cover the foundation, base plates, sole boards, standards, ledgers, transoms, braces, ties, guardrails, toe boards, platforms, access, and fall protection. Use a written checklist. Sign and date the checklist. Keep it on file. The second concept is the periodic inspection. Even if the scaffold is not altered, it must be inspected at regular intervals. The interval depends on the risk and the environment. A common standard is at least every 7 days. In harsh environments, such as coastal areas with salt air or dusty sites, inspect more frequently. After heavy rain, strong winds, or any impact, inspect immediately. The third concept is the post-alteration inspection. Any change to the scaffold, such as adding a lift, removing a tie, or changing a platform, requires a new inspection before use. Never assume that a small change is safe. The fourth concept is the tagging system. A tag is a visual indicator of the scaffold status. Use three colours: green for safe to use, yellow for caution or restricted use, and red for do not use. The tag should include the date of inspection, the name of the inspector, and any restrictions. Tags must be placed at all access points. In Africa, where literacy levels vary, use symbols as well as words. A green circle with a tick, a yellow triangle with an exclamation mark, and a red square with a cross are universally understood. The fifth concept is maintenance. Scaffolding components must be maintained in good condition. Inspect tubes for bends, cracks, and corrosion. Reject damaged components. Inspect couplers for thread damage and wear. Inspect boards for cracks, rot, and splits. Wooden boards are common in Africa but must be inspected carefully. Replace any board that is damaged. Store scaffolding materials in a dry, covered area. In many African sites, materials are left outside in the rain, which accelerates corrosion. Proper storage extends the life of the equipment and reduces cost. The sixth concept is record keeping. Keep a log of all inspections, maintenance, and repairs. This log should be available for review by supervisors, clients, and regulators. Good records demonstrate due diligence and can protect your company in the event of an incident. The seventh concept is training for inspectors. Inspectors must be trained and competent. They must understand scaffold design, load limits, and failure modes. They must be able to identify defects such as bent tubes, missing couplers, loose ties, and damaged boards. They must have the authority to stop work if a scaffold is unsafe. The eighth concept is the role of the supervisor. The supervisor must ensure that inspections are carried out and that tags are correct. The supervisor must also ensure that workers respect the tags. A red tag means do not use. No exceptions. The ninth concept is the role of the worker. Workers must report any damage or concern to the supervisor. They must not use a scaffold that is tagged red or yellow without authorization. They must not remove tags. The tenth concept is continuous improvement. Review inspection records to identify trends. If the same defect appears repeatedly, investigate the root cause. It may be a training gap, a material quality issue, or a design problem. Fix the cause, not just the symptom. In Africa, scaffolding inspection is often neglected because of time pressure and lack of awareness. But the cost of a collapse is far higher than the cost of inspection. A single fatality can shut down a project, lead to criminal charges, and destroy a company reputation. Inspection is not bureaucracy. It is risk management. In summary, inspect before use, inspect regularly, inspect after changes, tag clearly, maintain materials, keep records, train inspectors, and empower supervisors and workers. In the next lesson, we will cover advanced topics including design, loading, and special scaffolds.

lessons.title: Advanced Scaffolding: Design, Loading, and Special Applications
lessons.body: This final lesson in Module 2 covers advanced scaffolding topics: design principles, loading calculations, and special applications relevant to African construction. These topics are for engineers, senior supervisors, and scaffolders who want to deepen their competence. The first advanced topic is scaffold design. A scaffold is a structure, and like any structure, it must be designed to carry loads safely. Design involves calculating the loads, selecting the components, and checking stability. In many African countries, scaffolds are erected without design, based on experience alone. This is acceptable for simple, low-rise scaffolds, but not for complex, tall, or heavily loaded scaffolds. A competent person or engineer must design scaffolds that exceed certain height or load thresholds. The second topic is load types. There are dead loads, live loads, and environmental loads. Dead loads include the weight of the scaffold itself, including tubes, boards, couplers, and platforms. Live loads include workers, tools, and materials. Environmental loads include wind, rain, and in some areas, seismic activity. You must consider all three. The third topic is load combinations. Loads do not act in isolation. A scaffold may be subjected to dead load plus live load plus wind load simultaneously. Design codes provide load combinations that must be checked. The most critical combination often involves wind because wind can cause uplift and overturning. The fourth topic is wind loading. Wind is a major cause of scaffold collapse in Africa, especially in coastal cities and during storm seasons. Wind loading depends on location, height, and exposure. You must tie the scaffold to the building to resist wind. Ties must be designed to carry both tension and compression. In open areas, you may need additional ties or larger base plates. The fifth topic is foundation design. The foundation must support the scaffold without settlement. In weak soils, you may need to spread the load over a larger area using concrete pads or timber mats. In waterlogged areas, you may need to dewater or use piles. Never assume that the ground is strong enough. Test it or consult a geotechnical engineer. The sixth topic is tie design. Ties connect the scaffold to the building. They must be strong enough to resist wind and impact. Ties should be installed at regular intervals. The general rule is one tie for every two bays horizontally and every two lifts vertically. Ties must be installed as the scaffold is erected, not after. The seventh topic is special scaffolds. These include cantilever scaffolds, suspended scaffolds, and birdcage scaffolds. Cantilever scaffolds are used where the ground cannot support a standard scaffold. They require counterweights and strong anchors. Suspended scaffolds are used for high-rise facade work. They require rigorous inspection of ropes, hoists, and anchors. Birdcage scaffolds are used for large ceiling areas. They require dense tube grids and careful design. The eighth topic is mobile scaffolds. Mobile scaffolds are towers on castors. They must be used on level ground. Castors must be locked before use. Workers must not move the scaffold while on it. Mobile scaffolds must not be used on slopes or uneven ground. The ninth topic is access and egress for special scaffolds. Suspended scaffolds require a safe means of access at the top and bottom. Cantilever scaffolds require a safe platform and guardrails. Birdcage scaffolds require internal ladders or stairs. The tenth topic is emergency planning. For advanced scaffolds, you need a rescue plan. If a worker falls and is suspended by a harness, you must have a way to rescue them quickly. Suspension trauma can kill within minutes. Train your team in rescue procedures. In Africa, advanced scaffolding is increasingly needed for high-rise buildings, bridges, and industrial plants. But advanced scaffolding also carries higher risk. Do not attempt advanced scaffolds without proper design, training, and supervision. Invest in competent people and quality materials. In summary, this module has covered the fundamentals, types, erection and dismantling, inspection and tagging, and advanced topics. You now have a solid foundation in scaffolding safety and practice. Remember, scaffolding is not just equipment. It is a system that includes people, procedures, and planning. Build it right, inspect it right, and use it right. Your life and the lives of your workers depend on it.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaffolding Materials, Load Tables, and Site Logistics for African Construction

This module is written for the site supervisor, foreman, or small contracting business owner who needs to make fast, profitable, and safe decisions about scaffolding on real African construction sites. Whether you are working on a residential block in Kumasi, a warehouse in Nairobi's Industrial Area, or a road bridge in Lusaka, the principles are the same: know your materials, know your loads, and know your logistics before the first standard is erected. This reference consolidates practical figures, tables, and checklists you can use directly on site. All figures are drawn from published standards and institutional sources; where local conditions differ, always verify with the manufacturer or a qualified engineer.

Table 1: Safe Working Loads and Spans for Common Scaffold Components

The following table gives indicative safe working loads (SWL) for standard scaffold components under normal site conditions. Values assume steel tube to EN 39 or BS 1139, and timber boards to EN 12811. Always derate for wind, corrosion, or damaged material. For African sites where equipment is often reused, visual inspection plus a 20% derate is a prudent default unless a competent person certifies otherwise.

Component Typical Size Safe Working Load (kg) Maximum Span (m) Notes
Steel standard (vertical tube) 48.3 mm OD, 4.0 mm wall 3,000 per leg N/A (vertical) Assumes base plate on firm ground
Steel ledger (horizontal) 48.3 mm OD, 3.2 mm wall 1,500 uniformly distributed 2.1 m between standards Reduce to 1.5 m for heavy duty
Timber board (scaffold plank) 225 mm x 38 mm 250 per board (point load) 1.5 m support centres Grade 1 timber, dry condition
Aluminium mobile tower 1.5 m x 1.5 m base 750 per platform level N/A (free-standing) Max height 12 m outdoor, 8 m indoor
Coupler (right-angle) 48.3 mm 630 slip load N/A Torque to 50 Nm

Sources: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L; EN 12811-1; BS 1139; HSE GS28. Figures are indicative and must be confirmed against manufacturer data and a site-specific design.

For a small contractor pricing a job, the quantities below give a realistic starting point for a standard independent scaffold with 2.0 m lifts. Adjust for site geometry, access restrictions, and re-use. In many African markets, tube-and-coupler remains cheaper than system scaffold for small jobs, but system scaffold reduces labour time by 30â40% on larger projects.

Cost ranges compiled from regional supplier quotes (Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Ghana, 2023â2024) and cross-checked against ILO construction sector wage data. Localise before quoting.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Fall Hazards and Load Collapse

Falls from height remain the leading cause of construction fatalities worldwide. According to the WHO Falls fact sheet, falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury death globally, and construction workers are among the highest-risk groups. On African sites, lack of guardrails, missing toe boards, and untrained erectors are common contributing factors.

Never:

  • Erect scaffold above 2 m without guardrails, mid-rails, and toe boards on all open sides.
  • Use damaged, bent, or corroded tubes â a single failed coupler can collapse an entire lift.
  • Overload a platform beyond its rated SWL. One pallet of cement blocks can exceed 1,500 kg.
  • Allow untrained workers to erect or alter scaffold. Competency training is not optional.

If in doubt, stop work and consult a competent scaffold designer or engineer.

Quick Reference Checklist for Site Supervisors

  1. Design and load check: Confirm the scaffold is designed for its intended duty (light, medium, heavy) and that the ground bearing capacity supports the base plates. On soft African soils, use sole boards or concrete pads.
  2. Material inspection: Check every tube, coupler, and board for cracks, bends, corrosion, or previous damage before erection. Reject and tag out anything suspect.
  3. Foundation and base: Ensure base plates are seated on firm, level ground. On slopes, use adjustable base jacks and never pack with loose bricks or timber offcuts.
  4. Bracing: Install diagonal bracing in both directions at the base, and at intervals not exceeding 6 m vertically. Free-standing towers must be braced on all four sides.
  5. Platforms and edge protection: Every working platform must have guardrails at 1.0 m and 0.5 m, plus toe boards. Gaps between boards must not exceed 25 mm.
  6. Access: Provide a safe ladder or stair access every 30 m along the scaffold. Never climb the standards.
  7. Inspection and tagging: Inspect before first use, after any alteration, and at least every 7 days. Attach a dated tag showing status (green = safe, red = do not use).
  8. Training and supervision: Only trained and competent scaffolders may erect, alter, or dismantle. Supervisors must verify competency records.

Business-First Notes for African Contractors

Scaffolding is often treated as a cost centre, but it is a profit lever. Well-maintained tube-and-coupler stock can be reused across multiple projects, reducing hire costs by 40â60% compared to renting. In markets where import duties on steel are high, buying quality used scaffold from a reputable dealer and re-certifying it is often the fastest route to capacity. Keep a simple asset register: every tube, coupler, and board numbered and inspected monthly. This reduces loss (a major hidden cost on African sites) and supports faster mobilisation.

Labour productivity matters. A trained three-person crew can erect roughly 40â50 mÂ² of independent scaffold per day in good conditions. Untrained labour may take twice as long and produce unsafe work. Investing in a one-week competency course for two or three key workers pays back within a single medium-sized project through faster erection, fewer reworks, and lower insurance risk.

Finally, document everything. Photograph the scaffold before use, keep inspection records, and retain material certificates. This protects you legally if an incident occurs and strengthens your bid for larger contracts, where clients increasingly demand evidence of safety management systems.

Further Reading

  • US OSHA Scaffolding eTool â Comprehensive free guide to scaffold types, hazards, and inspection requirements.
  • UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) â Scaffolding â Practical guidance on erection, inspection, and load capacity.
  • ILO Construction Sector Safety and Health â International labour standards and safety guidance for construction workers.
  • WHO Falls Fact Sheet â Global data on fall-related injuries and prevention priorities.
  • NIST Materials and Structural Systems Division â Technical reference on structural materials and load testing.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a base plate on a scaffold?
options: A) To connect guardrails to the frame
B) To distribute the load over a larger area
C) To anchor the scaffold to a building
D) To provide a walking surface for workers
quiz.explanation: Base plates spread the scaffold load over a wider area to prevent sinking into the ground and improve stability.

quiz.q: Which component is used to connect two scaffold tubes at a right angle?
options: A) Swivel coupler
B) Putlog coupler
C) Right angle coupler
D) Sleeve coupler
quiz.explanation: A right angle coupler, also called a double coupler, joins two tubes at 90 degrees.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended height for a freestanding scaffold without tying to a structure?
options: A) Twice the minimum base dimension
B) Three times the minimum base dimension
C) Four times the minimum base dimension
D) Five times the minimum base dimension
quiz.explanation: Freestanding scaffolds are generally limited to four times the minimum base dimension unless otherwise specified by an engineer.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key inspection requirement before using a scaffold?
options: A) Checking that all workers have gloves
B) Confirming the scaffold was painted recently
C) Ensuring the scaffold is made of wood
D) Verifying that guardrails and toe boards are in place
quiz.explanation: Guardrails and toe boards are essential fall protection and falling object protection measures that must be verified before use.

quiz.q: What does the term toe board refer to on a scaffold?
options: A) A low barrier at the platform edge to prevent tools from falling
B) A board used to level the ground under the scaffold
C) A diagonal brace for lateral stability
D) A plank used as a walkway between platforms
quiz.explanation: Toe boards are low vertical barriers at the edge of a platform that stop tools and materials from falling off.

quiz.q: Which type of scaffold is suspended from overhead structures by ropes or cables?
options: A) Mobile scaffold
B) Suspended scaffold
C) Tube and coupler scaffold
D) System scaffold
quiz.explanation: Suspended scaffolds hang from overhead supports using ropes or cables and are often used for work on tall buildings.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a diagonal brace on a scaffold?
options: A) To support the platform planks
B) To attach the scaffold to a wall
C) To provide lateral stability and prevent racking
D) To serve as a ladder for access
quiz.explanation: Diagonal braces stiffen the scaffold and prevent it from twisting or racking under load.

quiz.q: When must a scaffold be inspected by a competent person?
options: A) Only after a near miss incident
B) Once every six months
C) Only when the scaffold is first erected
D) Before each work shift and after any alteration or adverse weather
quiz.explanation: Scaffolds must be inspected before each shift, after any modification, and following events like high winds or heavy rain.
